title: The Lease Clause That Pushed Sam Walton Out of Newport
dek: In 1950 Sam Walton lost his thriving variety store in Newport, Arkansas, because his lease had no renewal clause, and started again in Bentonville.

story.event: Losing the Newport, Arkansas, store when the landlord refused to renew the lease, and starting again in Bentonville
story.summary: In 1950 Sam Walton's landlord in Newport, Arkansas, refused to renew the lease on the Ben Franklin variety store Walton had run since 1945 and built into a regional leader; the lease had no renewal clause and the landlord wanted the store for his son. Walton sold the fixtures and inventory to the landlord for $50,000, moved to Bentonville and opened Walton's 5 & 10 there in May 1950.
paragraphs: In his fifth year running the Ben Franklin variety store on Front Street in Newport, Arkansas, Sam Walton found out what was wrong with his lease. It had no renewal clause, a standard protection he had not secured when he signed it in 1945, and his landlord, P. K. Holmes, would not renew at any price. Walton later called it the low point of his life: "I blamed myself for getting suckered into such an awful lease."

He had arrived without a day's experience of running a business. He paid $25,000 for the franchise, helped by a loan from his father-in-law, and only afterwards learned that the store was, in his words, "a real dog", with a rent of 5 per cent of sales. He watched the Sterling Store across the street, found suppliers cheaper than the franchise's own and cut prices to sell more. By his fifth year sales had roughly tripled, the loan was repaid, and he was president of the Chamber of Commerce. Three of the Waltons' four children were born in Newport.

Walton believed Holmes, who owned a department store in town, simply saw how well the Ben Franklin was doing and wanted it for his son. The business historian Richard Tedlow has suggested another irritant: Walton had taken over a building Kroger was leaving and opened a small department store there, mainly to keep his rival out. There was no other space in Newport to move to. Holmes bought the fixtures and inventory for $50,000, which Walton conceded was a fair price. Helen, who loved the town, was heartsick. Walton said he did not dwell on it, but added: "I know I read my leases a lot more carefully after that."

The family moved to Bentonville, a town of about 3,000 people, on 1 May 1950. With his father-in-law's help Walton bought the Harrison Variety store and opened it by 9 May with a one-day remodelling sale. He named it Walton's 5 & 10; by one count it was the third self-service variety store in the country. He opened the first Wal-Mart in 1962. In 1969 Wal-Mart No. 18 opened in Newport, and before long, he wrote, the old Front Street store closed.

quote.text: Every soul is by this intrinsic necessity quitting its whole system of things, its friends and home and laws and faith, as the shell-fish crawls out of its beautiful but stony case, because it no longer admits of its growth, and slowly forms a new house
quote.source_title: Essays — First Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2944
quote.connection: Emerson reads such breaks as growth: a shell outgrown, a new house slowly formed. Walton's later success seems to bear him out. But the Waltons had not outgrown Newport. Helen loved it, and they were pushed out over a missed clause. The loss and the growth were both real.

reflection: It would be easy to read this as a tidy lesson in setbacks becoming springboards. Walton did not tell it that way. He said it made him sick, he blamed himself and he was angry with the landlord; then he moved, and read his leases more carefully afterwards.

That order seems right. Some losses are partly your own doing, and owning that is different from punishing yourself for it. You can name the clause you missed, feel the unfairness of the rest, and still take the next practical step. Nothing requires you to call a loss good while you are standing in it.
invitation: Pick one agreement your work depends on, a contract, a lease or a service term, and read its renewal or termination clause today. Put the key date in your calendar, then close the file.

research_notes: Walton's own account is in his memoir Sam Walton: Made in America (1992), which is not freely available online; his words are quoted here as reproduced in Richard Tedlow's 2001 excerpt on HBS Working Knowledge, and the story attributes them to Walton. Sales figures differ: Tedlow gives $72,000 before Walton and about $250,000 in his fifth year (with a profit of $30,000 to $40,000); the Encyclopedia of Arkansas says $80,000 to $225,000 in three years. The story says only that sales roughly tripled. Tedlow gives Holmes's rent as rising from $3,600 to about $12,500 a year; not used. Some popular accounts describe the $50,000 as Walton buying the store; Tedlow's text is clear that Holmes bought the inventory and fixtures from Walton, which matches Walton's own 'fair price' remark, and the story follows it. The $50,000 rests on Walton's memoir via Tedlow only, so it is attributed rather than cross-checked. The exact month the non-renewal became known is not documented; the story says 'in his fifth year', and the family moved on 1 May 1950. The amount of the father-in-law's loan is not given in the sources used, so no figure is stated. Tedlow's suggestion that the Eagle Store may have counted with Holmes is presented as his suggestion; Walton's own explanation is that Holmes saw how well the store was doing. Wal-Mart No. 18 and the closing of the Front Street store come from Walton's memoir as quoted by Tedlow. The Emerson passage is from the essay 'Compensation'.
